tldr: Sepehrifar and Khodami argue that developer experience in large organisations is shaped less by platform programmes than by small, shared implementation details that developers themselves build and spread.
summary: Makan Sepehrifar (Productboard) and Soroosh Khodami (Rabobank) open by asking what developer experience actually is, then trace how it emerges as a company grows from a two-pizza startup to thousands of engineers. Teams split along domains, Conway's law turns org structure into architecture, departments optimise locally, and top-down alignment means managers agree on dependencies between developers who have never met. The result is process chaos and bureaucracy, which platform teams are created to fix by adding visibility and standardisation. The paradox, Sepehrifar says, is that these teams try to speed up delivery by becoming the new bottleneck.

He frames developer experience as three pulling forces: transformation programmes copied from books (adopting the Spotify model one-to-one), organisational history that resists because it was optimised per department, and developers caught in between who want predictability and autonomy. The anti-patterns he names are technical dictatorship (choosing tools from market research, then enforcing them with admin rights and compliance), wrapping every cloud service in an in-house abstraction that lags the provider and introduces new jargon, and portal-driven experience, where a logic-heavy Backstage-style portal becomes the only way in. Choosing the abstraction level is the hard trade-off: too abstract and developers cannot troubleshoot, too transparent and onboarding suffers.

For platform teams, Sepehrifar's advice is to accept that you always run behind developers, that silent customers are the happy ones, and that 100 developers have 101 preferences. His principles: build for composition and extension, co-create and co-evolve with developer communities, enable rather than enforce (adoption targets fall to Goodhart's law), and show empathy by giving up admin rights, chasing friction instead of market share, and meeting developers in the tools they already use. Khodami adds that platform teams must state what they support; his team spent much of its week debugging consumers' pipeline scripts. Capabilities should be granular APIs that others wrap as CI tasks, CLIs, MCP servers, skills or portal plugins.

Khodami's examples of bottom-up wins: Picnic's use of Google's Error Prone rules to end code-review bikeshedding, shared early and rewarded with stickers, which became a foundation of its Java platform and was open-sourced; a Rabobank tribe whose higher pipeline standards were extended to the whole organisation instead of being replaced; a parent POM that grew from 20 to 1,000 microservices and made OpenTelemetry onboarding a few-line change; and shared hardened Java base images. He also urges sharing articles, runbooks and failure stories, including his own team's artifact-management platform that took weeks to onboard. On AI, Sepehrifar says well-documented services and CLIs exposed via MCP let coding agents handle discoverability, and encoding conventions as skills made every PR in one old repository look alike.
keyPoints: Platform teams created to remove friction often become the organisation's new bottleneck.

Named anti-patterns: technical dictatorship (tool-first decisions enforced through admin rights and compliance), in-house wrappers over cloud providers, and portal-driven experience that puts logic in the UI before a solid backend.
Platform principles: build for composition and extension, co-create with developer communities, enable rather than enforce, and drop your own admin rights to feel developer friction.
Platform teams should define their support boundary; Khodami's team was spending most of its week debugging consumers' pipeline scripts.
Expose a capability as a granular API (for example a database-creation API) so others can build CI tasks, CLIs, MCP servers, skills and portal plugins on top.
Picnic standardised code style with Error Prone rules, started small, rewarded contributors with stickers, and later open-sourced the result.
A shared parent POM grew from 20 to 1,000 microservices and made OpenTelemetry onboarding a few-line change for all of them.
Coding agents reading well-documented CLIs and docs over MCP reduce the platform discoverability problem; conventions written as skills make PRs consistent.
takeaways: Turn something your team already built, such as a parent POM, hardened base image or pipeline template, into a shared component and advocate for it.
If you run a platform team, write down what you support and what is out of scope.
Publish runbooks and failure stories, not only code, after solving an incident or a hard onboarding.
Encode your repository conventions as agent skills or policies instead of relying on the model to infer them.
When you adopt an inner-source component, take responsibility for fixing it rather than only filing issues.

quotes.text: These platform teams are trying to accelerate delivery by becoming the new bottleneck of the organization.
For platform engineering teams, the happy customers are the silent customers.
If you ask 100 developers about their preferences, you will end up with 101 different preferences.

watchIf: You work in or alongside a platform team in a large organisation and want concrete ways to improve developer experience without waiting for a transformation programme.
